prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which established the basis for incretin-based therapy of type 2 diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize part on B045 with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. Having read the whole first round, I note that the six of us reached it by the same scientific route, and that no one disputes its maturity. The chain from the incretin effect and proglucagon processing, through the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, to receptor pharmacology and drugs with large randomized cardiovascular, renal and weight outcome trials is continuous and has been confirmed independently for about three decades. It is a discovery in physiology that became medicine. The citation names the physiology and the active form, so it rewards what was discovered, and the wording 'established the basis for' therapy acknowledges the drug development without crediting it as the achievement.
statement.case_against: The attribution remains the weak point and I do not think round 1 resolved it. Habener is not among the credited names, the Mojsov, Habener and Holst priority history is contested, and none of us has audited the primary record, so my third name is a judgment about the discovery core and not a settled fact. Excluding Knudsen also leaves a prize that stops one step short of the drugs patients actually take. If the committee decides that the achievement is the therapy rather than the hormone, the trio should change. A single part also leaves the credit for all of B045 resting on three names, with no room to repair the omissions.

responses.point: She moved from a Knudsen trio at opening to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and still finds Knudsen's exclusion uncomfortable; she would address it in the citation wording and not with a fourth name.
responses.response: Her movement narrows our difference to one name, and I agree with her way of handling the discomfort. The rules cap the credit at three, so the repair has to happen in the wording. I would keep the clause that the discovery 'established the basis for' incretin-based therapy, since it names the therapy as a consequence without making it the achievement. I would not go further and describe long-acting analogues in the citation, because that would imply the credit that the cap does not let us give. I share her caveat that the early peptide credit has to be checked against the primary papers, and I have not done that. If it showed that Mojsov's priority cannot be defended, I would replace her with Knudsen and not leave a gap.

responses.point: He accepts the B045 trio but wants the committee to record openly that Mojsov's place depends on a contested priority claim, and he regards Knudsen as the main alternative name; he keeps the unfolded protein response (B007) as his own first-choice alternative.
responses.response: I agree that the trio should not be called clean and that the uncertainty belongs in the committee's record. I would go further than I did in round 1: Knudsen is the named fallback and not a settled exclusion, and I would switch if the attribution review went against Mojsov. On B007, we both describe Walter and Mori as a clean two-person discovery, and I agree it is not premature. My difference is the one that remains in his own statement. Its disease relevance is largely correlative or preclinical, and PERK, ATF6, Ron and Kaufman fall outside the credited names, so it does not outweigh a discovery with proven benefit in patients. I would not object to it as a second part in a later year.

responses.point: She supports the same trio, stresses that high opening agreement is not merit because all six of us share similar recollections of the same priority history, and has the unfolded protein response as her first alternative.
responses.response: Her point about shared recollection is correct, and it applies to me. All six of us name Habener as unresolved and none claims to have checked the record, so agreement on Mojsov is weaker evidence than five first-place rankings suggest. That is why I describe my third name as a judgment. I do not think that argues for a two-part prize with B007, however. A second part would use a place out of three on the candidate whose medical consequence is weakest and whose credited names are most open to the omission charge. If GLP-1 stalls on the third name, B007 is a sound fallback, but that is a reason to keep it as an alternative and not a reason to add it now.

responses.point: The chair asks whether B045 alone is sufficient and, if not, whether B016 or B007 is the better second part; he considers a June-Sadelain pair more fragile than the version with Rosenberg because Rosenberg's work is adjacent to CAR design and Eshhar is not credited.
responses.response: I think B045 alone is sufficient. A second part forces the three-name cap to be split, and the cap is the problem with B045 already, since it excludes both Knudsen and Habener. If a second part were required, I would choose B016 over B007 because it is a new treatment modality with demonstrated patient benefit. I agree that the credit is the difficulty. June and Sadelain alone leave Rosenberg's adoptive transfer work and Eshhar's original CAR concept outside, and with Rosenberg the trio would no longer fit within three people in total beside B045. That is why I keep B016 first among my alternatives and not as part of the preferred configuration.

responses.point: He holds that Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active peptide is a discovery contribution and that Knudsen's work is company drug design, and he is wary of moving optogenetics up because of his own field.
responses.response: I agree with the principle that the prize should honour discovery over development, and I accept his reading of Mojsov's synthesis of GLP-1(7-36) as a discovery contribution that made the insulinotropic action testable. I would only add that this reading depends on the priority question, which he also calls unresolved. On optogenetics I take his caution about field bias and share it, since my own work is also in neuroscience. The credit problem is the decisive objection for me: any trio of the six names excludes Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenböck, and I cannot justify those exclusions scientifically. I do not move B004 into my configuration or onto my alternatives.

uncertainties: The priority among Mojsov, Habener and Holst for the active GLP-1 peptide is unresolved and I have not audited the primary papers; if it goes against Mojsov, Knudsen should take the third place.
Whether the committee reads the achievement as the physiology of the hormone or as the drug it led to; the answer decides between Mojsov and Knudsen and I cannot settle it from the evidence supplied.

Whether a single-part prize will seem sufficient, or whether the committee will want a second basic-science or modality part (B016 or B007) that the three-name cap cannot accommodate without splitting credit.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited name on the shortlist. My documented collaborations (Grillner, Ernfors, and a 2009 co-authored paper with Thomas Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons) do not involve a credited name, and I request no recusal. I note that the chair's summary lists the Perlmann paper, and that I remain unchanged from round 1.
